text: What happens when two keys in a hash map produce the same index?
options: The hash map refuses to store the second key
The hash map automatically deletes the first key
The hash map uses a secondary data structure to store both keys
The hash map only stores the last key
explanation: You are correct because when two keys collide, the hash map uses a secondary data structure such as a linked list or tree to store both keys, allowing for efficient lookup and retrieval of the associated values.

text: A hash map with separate chaining has a load factor that keeps rising. What degrades first, and why?
options: Lookup cost, because chains grow longer and each one is scanned linearly
Insert cost, because the hash function slows down as the table fills
Memory only, since chaining never affects the time complexity of a lookup
Deletion cost, because removing a key forces every later key to be rehashed
explanation: You are right that lookups degrade first: with chaining the buckets stay addressable in constant time, but each holds a longer list, so the scan within a bucket is what turns O(1) into O(n) at the limit.

text: Why does open addressing with linear probing suffer badly from primary clustering, where chaining does not?
options: Because linear probing must rehash the whole table on every collision
Because occupied runs merge, so any key hashing into a run pays the full length of it
Because linear probing cannot support deletion under any scheme
Because the load factor of an open-addressed table can never exceed 0.5
explanation: You identified the real mechanism: adjacent occupied slots coalesce into runs, and a key landing anywhere in a run probes to its end, so clusters grow superlinearly in a way per-bucket chains never do.

text: To keep the k largest numbers from a long stream, which structure do you maintain?
options: A min heap of size k
A max heap holding every element seen
A sorted array of every element seen
A queue of the k most recent elements
explanation: You are correct: a min heap of size k keeps the smallest of your current best at the top, so it is the one to evict when a larger number arrives.

text: Why is a min heap of size k preferred over sorting the stream, for n elements with k much smaller than n?
options: Sorting is O(n log n) time and O(n) space; the heap is O(n log k) time and O(k) space
Sorting cannot be applied to numeric data arriving in a stream
The heap gives the k largest in sorted order, which sorting does not
Sorting is O(n squared) in every practical implementation
explanation: You have the tradeoff right: the heap never holds more than k elements, so it bounds memory by k rather than n, and each of the n elements costs at most log k rather than log n.

text: Quickselect finds the k largest in O(n) average time, beating the heap's O(n log k). Why is the heap still the right choice for a stream?
options: Quickselect has a worse average constant factor than heap operations
Quickselect needs random access to the whole dataset, which a stream does not provide
Quickselect cannot handle duplicate values correctly
Quickselect is O(n) only when the data is already partially sorted
explanation: You spotted the constraint that decides it: quickselect partitions in place over a materialised array, so it needs all n elements at once, while a stream is single-pass and may not fit in memory at all.

text: In Floyd's cycle detection, how do the two pointers move through the linked list?
options: Both move one node at a time, starting from opposite ends
One moves one node at a time, the other moves two
Both move two nodes at a time, one starting a node ahead
One moves forward while the other moves backward
explanation: You are correct: the slow pointer advances one node and the fast pointer two, so if a cycle exists the fast pointer laps the slow one and they meet.

text: After the two pointers meet inside the cycle, how do you find the node where the cycle begins?
options: Move both pointers one step at a time from the meeting point
Reset one pointer to the head, then advance both one step at a time until they meet
Count the cycle length, then walk that many nodes from the head
Reset both pointers to the head and repeat with a larger step size
explanation: You have the standard second phase: the distance from the head to the cycle start equals the distance from the meeting point to the cycle start, so two pointers moving at equal speed from those two places meet exactly at the entry.

text: Why does Floyd's algorithm use a step ratio of 1 and 2 rather than 1 and 3?
options: A ratio of 1 and 3 fails to detect cycles of even length
A ratio of 1 and 2 closes the gap by exactly one node per iteration, so it cannot skip over the slow pointer
A ratio of 1 and 3 would make the algorithm O(n squared)
Only a ratio of 1 and 2 keeps the memory usage constant
explanation: You identified the invariant: with speeds 1 and 2 the separation shrinks by exactly one each step, so a meeting is guaranteed, and the head-to-entry distance identity the second phase relies on falls out of that same ratio.

text: What does memoisation add to a plain recursive solution?
options: It caches results of subproblems so each one is computed once
It converts the recursion into a loop automatically
It reduces the memory the recursion needs
It guarantees the recursion will not exceed the stack depth
explanation: You are correct: memoisation stores each subproblem's answer the first time it is computed, so repeated calls with the same arguments return immediately instead of recomputing the whole subtree.

text: Which pair of properties tells you a problem is a candidate for dynamic programming?
options: Optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems
Optimal substructure and a greedy choice property
Overlapping subproblems and a sorted input
A recursive formulation and a bounded input size
explanation: You named both conditions: the optimum must be constructible from optima of subproblems, and those subproblems must recur, or caching them buys nothing.

text: A problem has optimal substructure but no overlapping subproblems. What does that imply?
options: Dynamic programming still halves the running time
Divide and conquer fits, and a memo table adds overhead without saving work
The problem cannot be solved recursively at all
A greedy algorithm is guaranteed to be correct
explanation: You drew the right line: merge sort has optimal substructure and no repeated subproblems, so it is divide and conquer. Without recurrence there is nothing for the table to reuse, and it costs memory for no gain.

text: In a URL shortener, what is the core operation when a user visits a short link?
options: Look up the short code and redirect to the original URL
Re-hash the short code to reconstruct the original URL
Search every stored URL for a matching prefix
Ask the client to supply the original URL for verification
explanation: You are correct: the short code is a key, the service looks up the long URL it maps to, and answers with an HTTP redirect.

text: Why is a hash of the long URL, truncated to seven characters, a risky way to mint short codes?
options: Truncation makes the code impossible to look up efficiently
Truncating a hash reintroduces collisions, so two different URLs can claim the same code
Hashes are too slow to compute at write time
Hash output cannot be encoded in a URL-safe alphabet
explanation: You spotted the failure: a truncated hash has a small output space, so by the birthday bound collisions appear far earlier than intuition suggests, and a collision silently sends users to the wrong destination unless you check and retry.

text: You use a counter encoded in base62 for short codes. What is the main operational drawback at scale?
options: Base62 codes cannot be made shorter than ten characters
A single global counter is a write bottleneck and leaks your total link count
Counter-based codes cannot be stored in a relational database
Sequential codes make cache hit rates worse than random ones
explanation: You caught both halves: every write must serialise through one counter unless you shard ranges, and because codes are sequential anyone can decode two links to learn how many you have issued between them.

text: What distinguishes horizontal scaling from vertical scaling?
options: Horizontal adds more machines; vertical adds more resources to one machine
Horizontal adds more resources to one machine; vertical adds more machines
Horizontal applies to databases only; vertical applies to application servers only
Horizontal reduces cost; vertical always increases it
explanation: You have it the right way round: scaling out means more nodes behind a load balancer, scaling up means a bigger box.

text: What must change in your application design before horizontal scaling actually works?
options: Requests must be stateless, or session state must move to shared storage
The database must be switched to NoSQL
All endpoints must be made asynchronous
The application must be rewritten in a compiled language
explanation: You named the precondition: if a node holds session state in memory, a user's next request landing on a different node loses it, so state moves to a shared store or into a signed token.

text: Your stateless web tier scales out cleanly, but throughput plateaus anyway. What is the most likely cause?
options: The load balancer cannot distribute beyond a fixed number of nodes
A shared downstream dependency, typically the primary database, has become the bottleneck
Stateless services degrade as node count rises
Horizontal scaling stops working above a certain request rate
explanation: You followed the bottleneck: scaling the tier you can scale just moves the constraint downstream, and the single writable database is usually where it lands, which is what pushes you toward read replicas, caching or sharding.

text: What do the three letters of the CAP theorem stand for?
options: Consistency, Availability, Partition tolerance
Capacity, Availability, Performance
Consistency, Atomicity, Persistence
Concurrency, Availability, Partitioning
explanation: You are correct: consistency, availability and partition tolerance are the three properties the theorem relates.

text: For a payments system facing a network partition, which tradeoff is appropriate and why?
options: Choose availability, because a declined payment is worse than a wrong balance
Choose consistency, because serving a stale balance risks double-spending money
Choose partition tolerance over both, since it can be traded away independently
Choose availability, because payment systems are not affected by stale reads
explanation: You made the right call: money must not be created or spent twice, so a payments path refuses to serve rather than serve a balance it cannot vouch for.

text: Why is describing a distributed system as simply choosing 'CP' or 'AP' an oversimplification?
options: The tradeoff only applies during an actual partition; the rest of the time the real tension is latency against consistency
Partition tolerance is optional in any system inside one datacentre
Modern consensus protocols provide all three properties simultaneously
CAP applies only to relational databases, not to distributed key-value stores
explanation: You are pointing at what PACELC formalises: partitions are rare, and in their absence the live decision is how much latency you will pay for stronger consistency, which the CAP label alone hides.

text: What is the purpose of a rate limiter on a public API?
options: To cap how many requests a client can make in a time window
To compress responses so they transfer faster
To distribute requests evenly across backend servers
To authenticate clients before they reach the application
explanation: You are correct: a rate limiter bounds request volume per client per window, protecting the service from abuse and from one caller starving the rest.

text: What problem does a fixed window counter have that a sliding window or token bucket avoids?
options: It cannot support different limits for different clients
A client can send a full window's quota either side of the boundary, doubling the intended rate
It requires storing every individual request timestamp
It cannot be implemented without a distributed lock
explanation: You found the boundary burst: with a fixed window, the quota resets abruptly, so requests bunched at the end of one window and the start of the next pass a limiter that was meant to smooth them.

text: Across a fleet of API nodes, why is per-node rate limiting with a shared counter in Redis still imperfect?
options: Redis cannot store counters with expiry
Read-then-write on the counter races between nodes unless the update is atomic, and the network hop adds latency to every request
Redis counters lose precision above a few thousand requests per second
Per-node limiting always rejects more traffic than intended
explanation: You identified both costs: a non-atomic check-then-increment lets concurrent nodes each see the same under-limit value, which is why the increment and comparison belong in one atomic operation or Lua script, and every request now depends on a network round trip.

text: What is the clearest structural difference between a relational and a document database?
options: Relational stores rows in tables with a fixed schema; document stores flexible documents
Relational databases cannot be queried with an index
Document databases cannot store numbers, only text
Relational databases keep data in memory; document databases keep it on disk
explanation: You are correct: the relational model fixes a schema over rows and columns, while a document store keeps self-describing records whose shape can vary.

text: Your data is highly relational with many-to-many joins, and correctness matters more than write throughput. Which fits and why?
options: A document store, because denormalised documents make joins unnecessary
A relational database, because joins and transactional integrity are what it is built for
A key-value store, because it offers the lowest possible latency
Either, because the choice has no effect once data volume is large
explanation: You matched the workload to the tool: joins across many-to-many relationships and multi-row invariants are exactly what a relational engine with ACID transactions handles natively.

text: Teams often denormalise into documents to avoid joins. What cost does that shift onto the application?
options: Reads become slower because documents are larger
Duplicated data must be updated in every copy, so consistency becomes the application's responsibility
The database can no longer enforce uniqueness on any field
Documents cannot be indexed on nested fields
explanation: You named the real trade: denormalisation buys read locality at the price of write amplification, and with no foreign keys the burden of keeping copies agreeing moves into your code.

text: What is the first step after a browser is given a URL with a hostname it has not seen before?
options: A DNS lookup to resolve the hostname to an IP address
A TLS handshake with the hostname
Sending the HTTP GET request directly to the hostname
Opening a TCP connection to the hostname string
explanation: You are correct: the transport layer needs an IP address, so the name must be resolved through DNS before any connection can be opened.

text: In what order do these occur for a fresh HTTPS request?
options: DNS resolution, TCP handshake, TLS handshake, HTTP request
TCP handshake, DNS resolution, HTTP request, TLS handshake
TLS handshake, DNS resolution, TCP handshake, HTTP request
DNS resolution, TLS handshake, TCP handshake, HTTP request
explanation: You have the layering right: resolve the name, establish the TCP connection, negotiate TLS over it, then send the HTTP request inside the encrypted channel.

text: Why does HTTP/2 multiplexing not eliminate head-of-line blocking entirely?
options: HTTP/2 still limits each connection to one request at a time
A lost TCP segment stalls every multiplexed stream, because TCP delivers bytes in order
HTTP/2 streams are processed strictly sequentially by the server
Multiplexing only works when all responses are the same size
explanation: You located the blocking one layer down: HTTP/2 removes it at the application layer, but all streams share one TCP connection whose in-order delivery means a single lost packet stalls them all, which is what QUIC was designed to fix.

text: What does it mean for an API endpoint to be idempotent?
options: Repeating the same request has the same effect as making it once
The endpoint always returns the same response body
The endpoint never modifies any stored data
The endpoint can be called by multiple clients at the same time
explanation: You are correct: idempotence is about the effect on state, so a retried request must not apply the change twice.

text: How does an idempotency key make a payment endpoint safe to retry?
options: The server stores the key with the result and returns the stored result if the key is seen again
The server rejects any request carrying a previously used key
The client uses the key to encrypt the request body
The key tells the server how long to wait before retrying
explanation: You described the mechanism exactly: the first request commits and records its outcome against the key, so a retry after a lost response replays the same answer rather than charging again.

text: Two identical requests with the same idempotency key arrive concurrently. What is required for correctness?
options: Rely on the client to serialise its own retries
Insert the key under a uniqueness constraint in the same transaction as the effect, so the second is rejected or waits
Compare request bodies and drop the later one
Add a short delay before processing any request carrying a key
explanation: You caught the race: checking for the key and then acting leaves a window where both requests see it absent, so the key insert and the state change must commit atomically for the database to reject the loser.

text: An endpoint has become slow in production. What is the most useful first step?
options: Look at metrics and logs to find where the time is actually spent
Add more application servers immediately
Rewrite the endpoint's slowest-looking function
Increase the client's request timeout
explanation: You started with measurement: without knowing which stage consumes the time, any change is a guess that may not touch the real cause.

text: The endpoint got slower after a feature that lists orders with their customer. Which cause should you suspect first?
options: An N+1 query, issuing one customer query per order returned
The JSON serialiser has become slower with more fields
TLS termination is now costing more per request
The load balancer is routing requests unevenly
explanation: You picked the classic regression for that shape of change: iterating results and lazily loading a relation turns one query into one per row, so latency scales with result size.

text: Median latency is unchanged but p99 has doubled. What does that pattern point to?
options: A uniform slowdown affecting every request equally
Contention affecting a subset of requests, such as lock waits, GC pauses or connection pool exhaustion
An increase in total request volume with no other change
A misconfigured client timeout
explanation: You read the distribution correctly: a uniform cause moves the median too, so an unchanged median with a heavier tail means most requests are fine and a minority are queueing behind something contended.

text: How many threads execute JavaScript in a browser tab by default?
options: One
Two, one for rendering and one for scripts
One per open connection
As many as the number of CPU cores
explanation: You are correct: JavaScript runs on a single main thread, which is why blocking it freezes rendering and input until the current task finishes.

text: A promise callback and a setTimeout callback both become ready during the same task. Which runs first?
options: The setTimeout callback, because timers have priority
The promise callback, because the microtask queue drains before the next macrotask
Whichever was scheduled first, in registration order
They run concurrently on separate threads
explanation: You have the ordering right: after each task the engine empties the entire microtask queue, where promise reactions live, before taking the next macrotask such as a timer callback.

text: Why can a promise chain that recursively schedules more microtasks starve rendering?
options: Microtasks run at a higher operating system thread priority than rendering
The microtask queue must be fully drained before the browser can paint, so a self-refilling queue never yields
Rendering is blocked whenever any promise is pending
Microtasks force a synchronous layout on every resolution
explanation: You identified the starvation: each microtask can enqueue another, and the drain continues until the queue is empty, so the loop never reaches the point where the browser would paint.

text: Which change most directly reduces the time until a page first renders?
options: Reducing the size of render-blocking CSS and JavaScript
Adding more comments to the HTML for clarity
Increasing the server's response timeout
Moving images to a larger resolution
explanation: You are correct: the browser cannot paint until it has processed render-blocking resources, so shrinking or deferring them shortens the path to first render.

text: What does adding the `defer` attribute to a script tag change?
options: The script downloads in parallel and executes after HTML parsing completes
The script downloads and executes immediately, pausing the parser
The script is skipped entirely on slow connections
The script executes before the HTML parser starts
explanation: You have it: `defer` keeps the download off the critical path and delays execution until parsing is done, preserving document order between deferred scripts, unlike `async` which runs as soon as it arrives.

text: A page scores well on load time but poorly on Cumulative Layout Shift. What is the usual cause?
options: JavaScript bundles are too large
Images or embeds without reserved dimensions, so content reflows once they load
The server's time to first byte is too high
Too many DNS lookups during page load
explanation: You separated the metrics correctly: CLS measures visual stability, not speed, and it is driven by elements that arrive without space reserved for them, pushing already-rendered content around.

text: What is the virtual DOM?
options: An in-memory representation of the UI that is compared against the previous one
A browser API for updating the page without JavaScript
A separate rendering thread provided by the browser
A compressed copy of the HTML sent by the server
explanation: You are correct: it is a plain in-memory tree that the framework diffs against the previous version to work out the minimal set of real DOM updates.

text: Is the virtual DOM faster than direct DOM manipulation?
options: Yes, diffing in memory is always faster than touching the real DOM
No, hand-written optimal DOM updates are faster; the virtual DOM trades some speed for a simpler programming model
Yes, because it bypasses the browser's layout engine
No, because it re-renders the entire page on every state change
explanation: You resisted the myth: diffing is overhead on top of the same DOM writes, and its value is that you get near-optimal updates from declarative code rather than maintaining imperative patches by hand.

text: Why does using array indices as keys in a reordered list cause bugs?
options: Indices are not unique across sibling elements
The index of an item changes when the list reorders, so the diff matches the wrong elements and reuses their state
Index keys prevent the framework from reusing any DOM node
Keys must be strings, and numeric indices are rejected
explanation: You explained the mismatch: the key must identify the item, not the position. When positions shift, index keys make the reconciler pair up unrelated items, so component state and uncontrolled inputs follow the wrong row.

text: A model performs poorly on both training and test data. What does this indicate?
options: High bias, meaning the model underfits
High variance, meaning the model overfits
The test set is too small
The features have been scaled incorrectly
explanation: You are correct: failing on the training data itself means the model is too simple to capture the pattern, which is underfitting driven by bias.

text: Training error is very low and validation error is much higher. What is the appropriate response?
options: Increase model capacity so it can fit the validation set too
Reduce variance, through regularisation, more data, or a simpler model
Lower the learning rate and train for more epochs
Swap the training and validation sets
explanation: You diagnosed overfitting and matched the remedy: the gap between the two errors is variance, so constrain the model or give it more data rather than adding capacity.

text: Why does the classical U-shaped bias-variance curve not fully describe large overparameterised networks?
options: Bias and variance cannot be measured for neural networks
Test error can fall again past the interpolation threshold, a double descent the classical curve does not predict
Overparameterised models have zero variance by construction
The tradeoff applies only to regression, never to classification
explanation: You are pointing at double descent: as capacity grows past the point of exactly fitting the training data, test error can decrease a second time, which the single U-shaped picture does not account for.

text: Fraud is 2% of your dataset and your classifier reports 98% accuracy. What should you check first?
options: Whether it predicts the majority class every time
Whether the training set was shuffled
Whether the learning rate was too high
Whether the features were normalised
explanation: You spotted it: a model that always answers 'not fraud' scores 98% on this data while catching nothing, so accuracy alone cannot distinguish it from a useful model.

text: Which metrics are appropriate for this imbalanced fraud problem?
options: Precision, recall and the precision-recall curve
Accuracy and mean squared error
R squared and adjusted R squared
Training loss and epoch count
explanation: You chose metrics that focus on the rare positive class: precision and recall describe what happens on the 2% that matters, and the PR curve summarises the tradeoff across thresholds.

text: Why is a precision-recall curve preferred over ROC-AUC under severe class imbalance?
options: ROC-AUC cannot be computed when classes are imbalanced
The false positive rate has a huge negative denominator, so ROC stays optimistic while precision collapses
PR curves are invariant to the classification threshold
ROC-AUC only applies to multiclass problems
explanation: You identified the denominator effect: with negatives vastly outnumbering positives, many false positives barely move the false positive rate, so ROC looks strong while precision, which divides by predicted positives, shows the real cost.

text: In k-fold cross validation, how is the data used?
options: Split into k folds; each fold serves as validation once while the rest train
Split into k folds and the model is trained on one fold only
The same random 20% is held out k separate times
The model is trained k times on the entire dataset
explanation: You are correct: every fold takes a turn as the validation set, so each observation is predicted exactly once by a model that never saw it in training.

text: What is the main advantage of cross validation over a single train-test split?
options: It guarantees the model will generalise to production data
It averages over k splits, giving a lower-variance estimate that does not hinge on one lucky partition
It eliminates the need for a separate test set entirely
It reduces training time by using less data per fold
explanation: You have the statistical point: one split can be unrepresentative by chance, and averaging across folds gives an estimate with less variance and a sense of its spread.

text: Why is standard k-fold cross validation invalid for time series data?
options: Time series data cannot be split into folds of equal size
Random folds let the model train on future observations and predict the past, leaking information
Time series models cannot be retrained multiple times
Cross validation requires the target variable to be categorical
explanation: You caught the leakage: shuffling destroys temporal order, so the model sees the future during training and the score no longer reflects forecasting, which is why forward-chaining splits are used instead.

text: Which opening best answers 'tell me about a time you disagreed with a teammate'?
options: A specific situation, what the disagreement was about, and what you did
A general statement that you always try to get along with everyone
An explanation of why the teammate was wrong
A description of how your team usually handles disagreements
explanation: You picked the concrete answer: behavioural questions ask for one real incident with your actions in it, not a policy or a character description.

text: What do the four parts of the STAR structure stand for?
options: Situation, Task, Action, Result
Story, Timing, Approach, Reflection
Setup, Tension, Answer, Review
Scope, Team, Analysis, Resolution
explanation: You have the standard frame: situation and task set the context, action is what you personally did, and result is what came of it.

text: A disagreement answer describes the conflict and the outcome but never says what you personally did. Why is that weak?
options: It is too short to fill the expected answer length
The Action step is where the interviewer assesses your judgement, so omitting it leaves nothing to evaluate
It implies the disagreement was not serious enough to discuss
It fails to demonstrate technical knowledge
explanation: You located the gap that matters: the interviewer is assessing your behaviour, so context and outcome without your own decisions and reasoning give them nothing about you.

text: When asked about a project you are proud of, what must the answer make clear?
options: Your specific individual contribution
The full technical architecture of the system
The names and roles of everyone on the team
The total revenue the project generated
explanation: You are correct: the question asks what you did, so your own contribution has to be unmistakable within the team's work.

text: Why does answering entirely in 'we' weaken this answer?
options: It sounds insufficiently confident
It makes your individual contribution impossible to separate from the team's
It suggests the project was not technically difficult
Interviewers are instructed to reject collaborative language
explanation: You identified the real cost: 'we' describes the team's achievement, and the interviewer cannot score what they cannot attribute to you. Credit the team, then say what was yours.

text: What most strengthens the Result step of a project answer?
options: A statement that the project was well received by the team
A concrete measure of impact, such as a latency or error-rate change, and what you learned
A detailed list of every technology used
An explanation of what you would build differently with more time
explanation: You chose evidence over assertion: a measured outcome makes the impact verifiable rather than a claim, and the reflection shows you can evaluate your own work.

text: What is the interviewer primarily looking for when asking about a failure?
options: How you responded to it and what you took from it
Confirmation that you have never shipped a serious bug
Whether the failure was ultimately someone else's fault
How severe the technical failure was
explanation: You are correct: the question probes ownership and learning, so the response and the lesson matter more than the incident itself.

text: Why is 'I do not really have an example of a failure' a poor answer?
options: It reads as a lack of self-awareness or an unwillingness to take ownership
It is shorter than the expected answer length
It suggests you have not worked on enough projects
It implies your previous team had no quality process
explanation: You saw what it signals: everyone who ships has broken something, so claiming otherwise reads as either not noticing or not owning it, both worse than the failure would have been.

text: A candidate describes an outage they caused and ends with the systemic fix they introduced afterwards. Why is this strong?
options: It shifts responsibility from the individual to the system
It shows ownership plus a durable improvement, so the same class of failure cannot recur
It proves the original mistake was not really their fault
It demonstrates familiarity with incident tooling
explanation: You recognised the strongest shape: owning the mistake and then removing the conditions that allowed it shows you treat failures as system problems without evading your part in them.
